fields.v: Boonsri, R., Buranasaksee, U. (2025). A Repository-First Framework for Democratizing Chatbot Development. In: 2025 9th International Conference on Information Technology (InCIT), IEEE, pp. 775-782. https://doi.org/10.1109/InCIT66780.2025.11276047
Conference — 2025 9th International Conference on Information Technology (InCIT), IEEE, DOI 10.1109/InCIT66780.2025.11276047
Department of Science and Technology, Rajamangala University of Technology Suvarnabhumi, Nonthaburi, Thailand (both authors)

Proposes an approach; secondary: Compares — repository-first chatbot framework (layered Clean Architecture toolkit in C#/.NET with typed connectors, acceptance templates, scaffolds) paired with an AI coding agent driven by playbooks; compared with an agent-only baseline in a within-subjects controlled experiment (9 developers, 8 microtasks, 144 runs) plus a 50-user SUS study

Repository-first framework + AI coding agent ('Framework+Agent', F), no version; baseline Agent-only (A). Agent: ModelHarbor v3.25.10 VS Code extension in code mode, model qwen3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507, VS Code 1.103.0

Playbook filled by a domain expert (intent, slots, examples; predefined playbooks such as 'Weekly Plan Inquiry' with fields dates, descriptions, locations); framework repository with typed connectors, acceptance templates and code scaffolds; agent-generated handlers, routes, validators, test stubs; acceptance checklist with canonical prompts; recorded diffs and logs (transcripts, state deltas). All artefacts are plain Git files

End-user flow: (1) Playbook: select predefined playbook and fill fields; (2) Scaffold: agent analyses repository, generates C# code and wiring (webhooks, connectors, tests), runs smoke checks, fixes regressions; (3) Acceptance: canonical prompts executed, reviewer marks pass/partial/fail against a checklist; (4) Deploy: approved changes committed and deployed; later extensions as plugins

User reviews the diffs and accepts the changes (Scaffold step); reviewer (domain expert, team lead or QA; not a full-time developer, 'quality gate') marks acceptance outcomes pass/partial/fail against a checklist; approval before commit and deploy

Partly the full workflow: in the experiment professional developers used the framework codebase with per-microtask prompt stubs and the agent; acceptance by checklist audited by raters. The non-developer playbook flow was not exercised by citizen developers

Not classifiable (closest to spec-first: a filled playbook drives code generation, code is then maintained). Authors' wording: 'repository-first', agent 'compiles high-level specifications into versioned code artifacts'; they name 'specification-driven developments' only as a future enhancement
Feature additions: in F, to the existing framework codebase; in A, no framework code given (built without the scaffold)

8 microtasks (IDs 0101-0303) in 3 application-level tasks (3+2+3); each with isomorphic A/B variants; 9 developers × 8 microtasks × 2 conditions = 144 runs; 90-min cap per condition; SUS study with 50 users. Codebase size Not stated
Business chatbots on LINE Messaging with Google Sheets integration (greeting, location echo, nearby-places lookup); C#/.NET (ASP.NET Core, EF Core, PostgreSQL/pgvector, Redis)

9 professional developers recruited internally, mean 7.0 years experience (SD 2.05); 5 regular and 4 occasional users of AI coding tools; friendly competition with ~USD 60 voucher for the fastest. SUS study: 50 users (10 managers, 30 project support, 10 sales)

Time-to-completion per subtask (minutes); cost-to-completion (USD = tokens × provider's published price per million tokens, summed over all API calls in a trial); cost per minute (USD/min); token efficiency (output/input ratio); LLM calls and tool invocations; median feedback latency. Reported as A/F ratios of geometric means

Task success (pass/fail; partial = fail in primary analysis) against a pre-specified acceptance checklist per microtask; errors per 100 calls; QA accuracy normalised = Pass + 0.5 × Partial; first-turn resolution (FTR)
None (authors note time and cost do not capture code quality)
Developer time-to-completion; human interventions per 100 LLM calls; post-task developer survey (5-point Likert: satisfaction, perceived quality, perceived productivity; composite mean)
End-user usability: System Usability Scale (SUS) in a 50-user study, compared to the benchmark of 68

Automatic: VS Code extension (ModelHarbor) built-in logging of start/stop times per prompt, system and user prompts, responses, tool and command invocations, token counts, exit codes; cost computed from tokens and published prices. Manual: two raters independently audit chatbot behaviour against the written acceptance checklist, disagreements resolved by discussion (also described as adjudicated by the experimenter); post-task Likert survey; SUS questionnaire

(1) Framework+Agent (ModelHarbor v3.25.10 + qwen3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507): success criterion stated: microtask acceptance checklist fully satisfied; all retained runs completed within the 90-min cap and completion 'near-ceiling' (per-condition proportions not reported); QA accuracy 0.93, acceptance 0.89 (partial 0.08, fail 0.03), FTR 0.25, all within 2 turns (mean 1.70); SUS 70.6 vs benchmark 68; developer survey ≥3.9 on all dimensions. Absolute time and cost not reported (ratios only). Quality verdict: works (H1 supported against the checklist; SUS above the authors' 68 benchmark). Cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. (2) Agent-only baseline (same agent and model, prompt stubs, no framework): same checklist criterion; completion 'near-ceiling' overall, per-condition values not reported; relative to F took 2.29-2.48× the time, 1.76-1.88× the cost, 1.91× interventions per 100 calls, comparable errors; survey ≥3.9. Quality verdict: not determinable from the reported data (criterion stated, per-condition success not given). Cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors

Within-subjects crossover, AB/BA counterbalancing, 5-min washout; 8 matched microtasks with isomorphic A/B variants; 9 developers, 9 replications per microtask per condition (144 runs). Held constant: OS (Windows 11 build 26100), IDE VS Code 1.103.0, agent ModelHarbor v3.25.10, model qwen3-235b-a22b-instruct-2507, 10-15 min standardised briefing and prompt-library overview, prompt stubs (A participants free to adapt or bring their own prompts), 90-min cap. Acceptance tests: per-microtask checklist, two raters (blinded per threats section). Human intervention allowed and counted (per 100 calls). Trials with unrecoverable infrastructure failures excluded (pre-specified). Analysis on paired microtask log-ratios: geometric-mean ratios, bootstrap 95% CIs (B = 10,000), Shapiro-Wilk, t-test or Wilcoxon, Cohen's dz, Cliff's δ, McNemar, Holm for secondary outcomes. Power analysis: ~44% for a 20% and ~65% for a 25% time reduction

Framework+Agent better on time and cost: A/F time 2.44 [2.05, 3.02] (Table I; 2.48 in text; 2.29 [1.40, 3.63] = '56% faster' in abstract/H2); total cost 1.88 [1.56, 2.15] (Table I; 1.85 in text; 1.76 [1.12, 2.58] = '43% lower' in abstract/H2); human interventions 1.91 [1.45, 2.40]. No reliable difference in errors (1.14 [0.70, 1.95]), token efficiency (0.91 [0.81, 1.03]), latency (1.07 [0.73, 1.45]); cost per minute slightly lower for A (0.85 [0.73, 0.99]). 6 of 8 microtasks favour F; two low-complexity ones (0102, 0301) favour A. Significance judged from CIs excluding 1; p-values not reported. Break-even when tA/tF > rF/rA; frameworks essential beyond 3-4 integrations

Distinguished the conditions on time, cost and interventions, not on errors, token efficiency or latency. Results stated robust to alternative aggregation (all runs vs participant-level) and to scoring partials as successes. Limitations stated: underpowered with 8 paired microtasks in 90 min; learning/fatigue in crossover (mitigated); time/cost do not capture code quality; single stack (LINE, Google Sheets, C#/.NET); professional developers, not novices; residual biases. Future: mixed-effects models with task and developer random effects

Limitations: statistical power limited by 8 tasks in 90-min sessions; generalisation to other stacks uncertain; participants were professional developers, may not reflect novices; time/cost do not fully capture code quality. Gaps/future work: longitudinal studies with actual citizen developers; specification template integration (user stories, decision tables, 'specification-driven developments'); domain-specific playbooks; multi-organisation validation; broader task diversity

Inconsistencies: A/F time ratio 2.44 [2.05, 3.02] (Table I, V-B), 2.48 [2.05, 3.02] (V-A, limitations), 2.29 [1.40, 3.63] (abstract, H2); cost 1.88 [1.56, 2.15] (Table I), 1.85 [1.56, 2.16] (V-A), 1.76 [1.12, 2.58] (abstract, H2); SUS CI [68.6, 72.6] (Table I, abstract, Table IV) vs [68.6, 75.9] (H3); success adjudicated 'by two raters' (IV-G) vs 'by the experimenter' (IV-L), blinded raters claimed in threats; Takeaways claim reduced latency and improved token efficiency while Table I shows comparable values; QA scenarios in Table III (Check-in & Proof, Plan Modification, Sales Inquiry, Weekly Plan Ingestion) do not match the experiment microtasks; conclusion speaks of citizen developers although participants were professional developers. Values used here: Table I and the abstract/H2 as labelled. Replication: text says prompts, task variants, log schemas and acceptance tests were released and the implementation is open source, but no link is given. Pre-registration: not claimed (outcomes and exclusions called 'pre-specified'). Ethics: exempted. Programming language: C#/.NET
